title: Left Hanging Behind
text:
The young man finishes his scribblings on a paper. The handwriting is neat and meticulous - certainly unusual for him. The papers are stacked and laid neatly on the desk. Out from him is a long sigh. He walks to the window, silently and slowly. He stands there and simply watches.
The man was twenty-six years old.
He has been standing at the window for some time and frankly, he could not have told you how long if asked. Time has been acting weird lately - it moves untimely. A clock always ticks and tocks. It’s an unwritten law of time that it is constant and always continuing. But not his time - his time is elastic. It stretches and compresses until hours become minutes and minutes become hours. It all melts and fizzes up, becoming incomprehensible until it disappears altogether and he surfaces from it the way you surface from shallow water, gasping for air and unsure of how long he was under.
He used to love this town. Everything used to be so new. New job. New faces. New friends.
The street is doing what streets normally do. A woman walks with a stroller. A teenager on his phone, his eyes glued to it as he crosses the road. A kid holding her mother’s hand, both smiling and talking. All of them going somewhere, and mattering, to another or themselves. He observes them with a scientific curiousity - the way they move through the world as if the world is simply there, as if its continued existence is a thing you can rely on - no maintenance, no faith. He used to do that, taking it all for granted. He can’t remember when he stopped.
He had just moved into the apartment some years ago. He loved his apartment.
The apartment is clean. It’s not like it was dirty or messy before, but it was simply never this clean. He woke up this morning and cleaned it with a thoroughness that even surprised him - it was alike his usual cursory pass but more deliberate. The dishes, the desk; all tidied up. The towels and jackets hung properly on the rack for once, not just draped across. The bed was even remade and the corners smoothed and tightened. The room is fragrant; there is a hint of rosewood in the air, by virtue of the incense a friend had gotten him. He loves it, a lot, and wonders to himself why he had saved it all this time. His room is sparkling, so meticulously tidied with a care that he hasn’t paid it in months or perhaps years. He doesn’t ask himself why he is doing this now. He doesn’t care, or rather he doesn’t want to answer.
The incense was a gift from someone he cared about. The first gift he ever received from them. He couldn’t bring himself to use it because using it meant losing it - and he had so little left of them to lose. He needed it. To remind himself of happier times. To remember happiness.
His phone is on the desk. On it, there are three unsent messages. Who are they addressed to? It doesn’t matter. He just needs someone to read them. He wants -
He won’t let his mind do this to him again. He looked at the messages for a long time this morning and had turned the phone face down and not touched it since. They don’t say what he wants to say. He doesn’t know what he wants them to say. He doesn’t even know if language is sufficient for what he needs it to do anymore. His heart races. It is always like this now - restless like a bird throwing itself against a cage. He can’t recall the last time it was quiet.
He was sleep-deprived, but it was not his fault. The nightmares left him no other option.
He was eating too little too. He had no appetite. He couldn’t have had an appetite. But he did eat half a toast this morning and he smiled at the thought of it. It was an accomplishment to be celebrated.
He finally turns from the window. Something caught on the edges; something that is in his hand. He’s been holding onto it, turning it over, fiddling with it, without registering that he’s been doing it. His fingers have been at it the way fingers work at worry beads or rosaries, a nervous unconscious industry. He looks down at it and then looks away quickly, at the middle distance, at nothing. He doesn’t want to see it; he doesn’t want to contemplate it; he doesn’t want to acknowledge it.
Again, his heart is doing something irregular. No, not painful. Just so dull, just - present in a way that hearts usually aren’t, so unyielding in announcing itself, so demanding in being noticed. But it’s impossible. Its master is too weak, too docile, too scared. No one can know. He offers a silent apology to his heart.
Too much throbbing. The dullness pounded harder and harder. It wanted to be heard. No, it must be heard.
He sits down on the edge of the bed. He breathes. He gets up, shuffles awkwardly, then sits down again.
The light through the curtains is at an angle it always gets to in the late afternoon. He knows this light but he has only recently come to know this specific quality at this intensity. It is a beautiful light, the way it spreads across the floor, makes ordinary things briefly more than themselves and warms the room just right. It is ephemeral but cosmically incomprehensible. A ball of fire, millions of miles away, and yet its heat finds his skin. He has always loved this light without ever thinking to say so. This seems important suddenly. He doesn’t understand why.
The thing in his hands was not complicated by any means. Yet, it took him longer than it should have. Was it indecisiveness or a silent pleading that perhaps something would change? His hands kept stopping, undoing it, starting over. The fingers wouldn’t cooperate. Something in his body’s fine motor system was staging a quiet resistance - involuntary and futile. He continued anyway.
He is tired. That’s the truest thing he knows about himself since last year - the bone-deep exhaustion of being himself, of carrying the weight of his own continuing presence in the world, of not knowing what’s next, of waking up every morning and finding it still there, all of it, nothing changed, of having to slog through everything again, of having to play a role that he can never fill. He is tired of the effort. Tired of pretending that the effort is normal. It is not humanly possible, he thinks. He doesn’t understand how someone can live like this and act as if it’s fine.
He sighs. A bad habit of his that he picked up not very long ago.
He thought to himself that he was wasting too much time. He started to grow restless.
He gets up and walks to the closet to pick up a stool. He shouldn’t mess up the bed any longer. The closet door sticks out slightly, as it always has, in the way he has promised to fix but never did. He pulls it open. He always keeps a stool for when visitors come. There have been fewer of those lately. He reaches for it. Stops. What stopped him wasn’t the stool. It was a Bible. Not dramatically - it didn’t fall on him, didn’t catch the light in some cinematic fashion. It’s just there, sitting on the stool, slightly crooked and caked with a layer of dust. Why is it here? When was the last time he opened it? Didn’t his faith define him in the past? Didn’t God mean something to him once? He doesn’t remember how it all changed.
He is not a praying man anymore. He’s not sure when he stopped either - it belongs to the same period as everything else he lost track of - lost to the torpid attrition of the things that once held him together. Yes, he once knew this book.
though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
The verse surfaces without permission. He didn’t reach for it - it reached for him. He can see the room where he read it. A Saturday afternoon, someone’s living room, sitting together on the floor because there weren’t enough chairs. He sees the smiles of others - he doesn’t remember who. Hasn’t seen them and never bothered to contact. He was laughing at something with them - he doesn’t remember what. But he would not forget the laughter; and the experience of being there in the room with those people on that afternoon with no reason to be anywhere else.
He stands there by the stool, the verse sinking itself into his mind - though I walk through the valley - and what strikes him, standing here now, is the walking. Not the fear, not the comfort, not the rod nor the staff. The walking. That whoever wrote it was still moving. Still putting one foot in front of the other through the worst of it, through the valley and its shadow. He takes the Bible and the stool out.
He doesn’t know why he grabbed the Bible. Nonetheless, he leaves it on his table.
For some reason, his hands have stopped trembling.
That’s new. They were trembling all morning, through the cleaning, through the messages he didn’t send, through the sitting down and getting up and then sitting down - and now they’ve stopped, and in their steadiness there is something that feels almost like peace. He is still terrified, of course, but now assured.
He looked around the room.
He looks around the room.
The coffee mug with its ring on the wood. The books that he had painstakingly collected. His piano and all his other instruments that he had stopped playing. The phone face-down on the desk, those three messages still unsent. These things will continue like this after. They will be here exactly like this but he will not be here to see them.
The light at this hour, especially.
He looked at the light for a long time.
He looks at the light for a long time. A very long time. He would engrave it onto his retina if he could.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Pluck the open A string on a guitar, and a tuner will tell you it’s 110 Hz, meaning the string swings up and down 110 times every second. This count is called the frequency.
Here is a recording of the open A string, plucked three times.
Your browser does not support the audio element.
However, even though the note’s frequency is 110 Hz, it actually isn’t just purely one frequency. If it was really just that, it would actually sound more like this pure sine wave instead (You may need headphones for this and careful with the volume):
Your browser does not support the audio element.
You may think it’s just because the string is imperfect, friction, or air resistance. but the real reason why a guitar note sounds the way it does is because of harmonics. To see harmonics, we can analyze the frequency components of the sound using a spectrogram.
A spectrogram shows which frequencies are present at each moment, and brighter indicates higher energy. Below is the spectrogram of the plucked string:
Spectrogram of the recorded A string. Dashed lines mark the fundamental \(f_1\) and harmonics \(f_k = kf_1\).
For comparison, here is the spectrogram of the pure 110 Hz sine wave. Only the fundamental shows up:
Spectrogram of the pure 110 Hz sine wave. All the energy sits at the fundamental.
The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the fundamental, which sets the tone we hear, and both spectrograms share it. However, the plucked string differs by having energy level at frequencies not just at the fundamental, these frequencies are called harmonics. A property of harmonics is that they occur at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, our original note.
So here’s two questions that you may naturally raise:
We will start with the first question, as its answer will be helpful for the second question.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
A rope example
Before tackling harmonics head on, it may be helpful to think of a guitar string as a rope tied to a post, with you holding the other end and shaking it.
If you shake it at just the right rhythm, the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as often and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as often gives three loops. At any rates in between, no clean pattern builds up and the rope just jiggles. How often you shake is a frequency, and these special frequencies are exactly the fundamental and its harmonics.
In physics, these patterns are called modes, and the points that never move, including the two ends, are called nodes. An up-loop followed by a down-loop makes one full wave, and its length is called the wavelength \(\lambda\). So one loop is half a wavelength.
The figure below shows each mode as a snapshot. In reality, each loop keeps flipping between up and down, while the dots stay perfectly still.





The first four modes of a string with a fundamental \(f_1\) of 110 Hz. The dots are nodes, and \(n\) is the number of loops. Each color marks one full wavelength, so at \(n = 1\) the string holds only half a wavelength.










NoteWatch this for a visual demonstration at around 2:34.









Notice that the frequencies in the graph, 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz, are all multiples of 110. So then, why specifically multiples?
Suppose the string has length \(L\). Both ends are held fixed on the resting line, the straight line the string lies along when it’s still, so the wave pattern has to start and end on the ends.
Starting from the resting line at the left end, the pattern only returns to it at the end of each loop. If the string’s length ended partway through a loop, the right end would be sitting above or below the line, which is physically impossible, as the ends are fixed.





Top: a pattern with 2 loops starts and ends on the resting line, so it fits the string. Bottom: a pattern with 2.5 loops ends at a peak, leaving the right end displaced (arrow).




So a mode must contain a whole number of loops. To write this as a formula, recall that one loop is half a wavelength. A mode with \(n\) loops therefore fills the string when:
\[
L = n \cdot \frac{\lambda}{2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\lambda = \frac{2L}{n}
\]
Even though the loops seem to stay in place, each pattern is really made of ripples running back and forth along the string, bouncing off the fixed ends. These ripples travel at one fixed speed \(v\), determined by the string’s tightness and weight.
For any wave, frequency is speed divided by wavelength: the faster the wave moves, or the shorter it is, the more times it vibrates each second. For mode \(n\), whose wavelength is \(\lambda_n = 2L/n\):
\[
f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1,
\qquad\text{where } f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}.
\]
The speed \(v\) and the length \(L\) are fixed by the string, so only \(n\) changes from mode to mode. For an ideal string, mode 2 therefore vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at three times, and so on. (Real strings are slightly stiff, which nudges the higher harmonics a bit higher in frequency.) For our 110 Hz string, that gives 110, 220, 330 Hz.
This is also why turning a tuning peg changes the pitch: tightening the string makes waves travel faster, which raises \(v\), and with it every \(f_n\).
That settles the first question: a string can only vibrate cleanly at \(f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots\). But in the rope example we only saw these patterns one at a time, each at a rhythm we chose. When we pluck a string, all these modes appear at the same time, each at a different strength. So what’s happening?

title: On Harmonics.
section: Where are the harmonics coming from?
text:
Where are the harmonics coming from?
In the rope example, each pattern needed its own shaking rhythm: one loop at one rhythm, two loops at twice that. But a pluck has no rhythm at all. You pull once and let go. So where do all those modes come from?
If you’ve seen those viral clips of a guitar string vibrating in slow, lazy waves, you might now think the rope example is exactly what a guitar string does. And now you are demanding a refund of your time from me, because if guitar vibrates like the rope, then how can there be harmonics when a wave can only vibrate at one frequency?!?!
Hear me out before you get your pitchfork. It’s not quite like that. Many of those clips are filmed on a phone held inside the guitar, and those ripples are an illusion. Phone camera captures the picture line by line rather than all at once, so different parts of the string are photographed at slightly different moments.






NoteWatch this video at 01:46 to see the illusion.









So what does a plucked string really look like? Think about what your finger does. You are not shaking the string. You hook it with your finger, pull and let go. At that moment, the string forms a triangle: it is no longer a smooth curve, but two straight lines meeting at a corner, right where your finger is.





A guitar string is actually a triangle now?




That corner is the key to unlocking the mystery behind harmonics. To see why, we first need a closer look at how a mode moves.
A mode only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped upside down. Freeze it at any moment and you’ll see the same curve, just scaled. But at the end, it must return back to how it started. Therefore, a mode at any moment is a scaled version of its initial and final displacement. And a sine wave is the only curve that has this special property.






NoteWhy only a sine wave?





A tight string naturally wants to straighten itself because of tension. Wherever it’s bent, it gets pulled toward the inside of the bend, and the sharper the bend, the harder the pull. A straight stretch feels no pull at all.
For a string to keep its shape, the pull has to be strongest where the string is farthest out and fade to nothing where it crosses the middle, so that every point reaches the resting line at the same time.
A sine wave has the special property where the bend at every position is proportional to its height. It is most sharply bent at its peaks, and perfectly straight where it crosses the line. Therefore, the force exerted toward the resting line is proportional to the height.



However, the triangle is not a sine wave. Furthermore, look at the triangle, its straight sides will not feel any pull; the only bend is at the corner. As a force is only induced at a bend, the corner should start moving while the sides wait, and the triangle wouldn’t keep its shape.
Let’s test this prediction by releasing two strings side by side: one shaped like the third mode, and one shaped like the triangle.









  
  
    
    
      
          
      
        
      
          
      
          
      
          
      
          
      
          
      
          
      
          
    
    
      
      Once
      
      Loop
      
      Reflect
    
  




Both strings over one full period of the open A string. The dashed line is each string’s starting position.


The sine string behaves exactly as predicted: it only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped. However, the triangle behaves completely different, its corner splits into two that run off in opposite directions, and the straight parts only start moving once a corner reaches them. Freeze it at any moment and you’ll see a different shape, not a scaled triangle.
But also, watch the clock. After exactly one period, about 9.1 ms, the two corners have bounced off the ends and met again where they started, and the triangle is back to its original shape again.
So the triangle isn’t a mode, yet its motion repeats at exactly the fundamental’s rhythm like how a mode would. That is a hint of what the triangle might be.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Fourier Series
For some bookkeeping, we need to introduce a few formula.
Suppose we pluck the string at position \(p\), pulling it up to height \(h\). The starting shape is a triangle (as shown in the demonstration before): \[
\varphi(x) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{h\,x}{p}, & 0 \le x \le p \\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{h\,(L - x)}{L - p}, & p < x \le L
\end{cases}
\] Recall that each mode is a sine wave with \(n\) loops. The starting shape can be described as below. For the derivation, see Appendix A:
\[
X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]
In the 1750s, Daniel Bernoulli proposed that the motion of a string fixed at both ends is a sum of its modes. Not everyone was convinced, and Leonhard Euler and Jean d’Alembert certainly weren’t.
D’Alembert doubted that a corner was even allowed, since the equation for a vibrating string needs the string to be smoothly curved everywhere. Euler was happy to allow corners, after all, strings are plucked and harmonics are heard, but he couldn’t see how smooth sine waves could ever add up to one discontinued corners. If a finite sum of sines is smooth, then how can an infinite sum suddenly turn non-smooth? [1]
A breakthrough comes in the early 1800s. While studying how temperature changes over time inside a solid body, Joseph Fourier made an even bolder claim. He proposed that any shape can be written as a sum of sines, including our triangle. Mathematicians now call this a Fourier series. \[
\varphi(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
\]
Each \(b_n\) describes how much of mode \(n\) is in the triangle.
To reconstruct our triangle, we would need to find what is the contribution of each modes.
To find one of them, say \(b_3\), we need to isolate the third mode from all the others. We do this by exploiting a property of modes called orthogonality.






TipWhat is orthogonality?





Take two functions \(f\) and \(g\) on the string, \(0 \le x \le L\). Multiply their values at each point along the string, then add up all the results. This gives a single number, called the inner product \(\langle f, g \rangle\), defined as the integral \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,dx\). If \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\), we say \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal.
The modes are orthogonal to each other: for two different modes, the positive and negative products cancel out exactly when added up. A mode paired with itself gives \(\langle X_n, X_n \rangle = L/2\).
For those familiar with linear algebra, this is the dot product \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_i u_i v_i\), applied to functions. As an exercise, you can show that the continuous functions on \([0, L]\) form a vector space, and that \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\) behaves like a dot product.



Due to orthogonality, if we multiply the whole sum by \(\sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right)\) and add up the result along the string, every term except the third adds up to zero:
\[
\langle \varphi, X_3 \rangle = b_3 \langle X_3, X_3 \rangle
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b_3 = \frac{\langle \varphi, X_3 \rangle}{\langle X_3, X_3 \rangle} = \frac{\langle \varphi, X_3 \rangle}{L/2}
\]






TipAn analogy in vector spaces.





Let \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^3\). They are orthonormal: \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), and \(\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_i = 1\). Any vector can be written as \(\mathbf{v} = v_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2 \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3 \mathbf{e}_3\), where \(v_1, v_2, v_3\) are the scalar multiples.
We can recover \(v_2\) by taking the dot product with \(\mathbf{e}_2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{e}_2 &= v_1 (\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_2 (\mathbf{e}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_3 (\mathbf{e}_3 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) \\
                              &= v_1 (0) + v_2 (1) + v_3 (0) = v_2
\end{aligned}
\]



The same trick works for every mode, and we can derive a general formula for \(b_n\):
\[
b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \varphi(x)\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx
\]
We can now solve this integral to find what each \(b_n\) is.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
Simulating the harmonics
With the general formula, here are the first 16 modes for a string plucked a quarter of the way along, each scaled by its \(b_n\):





The first 16 mode for a string plucked at 0.25, each scaled by its \(b_n\). The black line is the triangle.




The fundamental, the blue hump, is the largest, but it peaks in the middle of the string, not at the pluck point. This is where the other modes, or harmonics come into play.
The 2nd mode, in orange, is much smaller. It is positive on the left half and negative on the right, so it pushes the shape up near the pluck point and down on the far side. The third mode is smaller again, and the higher harmonics shrink quickly. By the 16th they are barely visible.
Now let see what happens if we add the modes one at a time. Every curve below adds one more mode to the curve before it.





Each curve adds one more mode to the curve before it. The black line is the exact triangle.




The fundamental alone is a poor match for the triangle, but adding the 2nd mode pulls the peak towards the pluck point. Every mode after that makes a smaller adjustment, which slowly pulls the string to the side of the triangle.
The last part to form is the corner. Even with 16 modes, the peak is still slightly rounded. Whereas the smooth sides of the triangle need only a few modes, the sharp corner needs many high modes working together. This was the heart of Euler and d’Alembert’s objection: no finite number of smooth sine waves can ever make a perfectly sharp corner. At the same time, we see that we are getting closer to a triangle.
But \(b_n\) also depend on where the string is plucked. Change where you pluck and you change how much of each mode contributes to the triangle.





Adding modes 1 to 16 for three pluck points. Plucked in the middle, the curves settle almost immediately. Plucked near the end, many high modes are needed before the sharp corner forms.




You can try this right now at your guitar!
Pluck an open string right next to the bridge and you get a harsh, pinched, twangy “eeee”. The reason being that pluck point excites lots of high harmonics as the sharp corner is at the end of the string. The fundamental carries a smaller share of the shape, and the higher harmonics carry much more, which together forms harshness.
Now pluck the same string over the 12th fret, exactly halfway along. The sound is dominated by the fundamental with little odds harmonics, and the curves settle onto the triangle almost immediately: this leads to a softer, rounder, hollow sound.
Remember that Fourier’s claim is we must take the sum to infinite terms to make it exactly equal, so let’s take his advice to heart and sum the terms to infinity. Of course, it is obvious that we cannot compute an infinite amount of modes, but we can just take it to a large enough term, say 100, 1,000 and 10,000 terms:





Adding 100, 1,000 and 10,000 modes for three pluck points. At original size the curves are indistinguishable from the triangle; Right side shows the triangle corner zoomed (25x).




All it takes is just 10,000 modes and we are pretty much exact. There wasn’t even a need for infinity.
At full size, the three curves are indistinguishable from the triangle. The only place they differ is the corner, and it is only visible at 25x zoom. At 100 modes, the corner is still visibly rounded. At 1,000, there is a small ripple but otherwise quite close. At 10,000, the curve is indistinguishible.
So that settles the old argument. Euler and d’Alembert were right that no finite number of smooth sine waves can make a perfectly sharp corner. But Fourier was right too: we just need an infinite amount of terms, or at least a large enough amount of terms.

title: On Harmonics.
text:
What even is infinite modes?
Now I hear you ask: Does nature actually generate infinite modes at plucking? Wait a second, does infinity even exist and if it does, what does it even look like?
For existence of infinity, I recommend you to consult your nearest philosophy professor or talk to a psychatrist. But the first question is answerable. We just need do some mathematics (actually physics.)






WarningBeware. Heavy maths start here.






So do infinite modes exist in real life?
Short answer: No, but for our ears finite modes is already good enough even at small terms. Here’s the long answer:
Our Fourier model treats the string as a continuum: a state where matter fills space smoothly, is infinitely divisible and so describable with densities. For example, the mass of a piece of string between \(a\) and \(b\) is modeled as a mass density function:
\[
m_{[a,b]} = \int_{a}^{b} \mu(x)\,dx
\]
Every point \(x\) along a continuum can move on its own, such a string has infinitely many degrees of freedom, and therefore infinitely many modes.
But these are just idealizations. A real string, however, is atoms held together by electromagnetic forces.
As a first approximation though, we can model it as a chain of atoms of mass \(M\), joined by massless springs with spring constant \(\lambda\), with both ends fixed. Each moving atom is one degree of freedom, so a chain of atoms has exactly as many modes as it has moving atoms. If \(N\) is the number of spacings between atoms, the frequency of mode \(m\) is:






TipHow is degree of freedom related to modes?





it may be helpful to think of modes as the number of peaks. A peak can only be formed if there’s an atom to create it.



\[
\omega_m = 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{m\pi}{2N}\right), \qquad m = 1, 2, \dots, N-1 .
\]
If we suppose \(N\) to be some unimaginably big number, then for \(m \ll N\), the chain is essentially smooth and under small-angle approximation, we have \(\sin(\theta) \approx \theta\), so \[
\omega_m \approx 2\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}} \cdot \frac{m\pi}{2N} = m \cdot \underbrace{\frac{\pi}{N}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{M}}}_{\omega_1} = m \cdot \omega_1
\]
and we recover the harmonic series \(f_m = mf_1\). It’s only when \(m\) gets close enough to \(N\) and the wavelength shrinks to just a few atoms, does the error become non-negligible.
So how close is “close enough”? Let’s conduct a thought experiment.
Take a 65 cm guitar string and assume that it is perfectly elastic. Its atoms are about 0.25 nm apart, so \(N \approx 2.6 \times 10^9\). As the number of atoms determine the number of modes, the string has at most a few billion modes.
In the best case, human hearing reaches about 20,000 Hz, so the highest harmonic you can hear on a 110 Hz string is at around \(m = 181\). At that mode, \(\theta = \frac{m\pi}{2M}\approx 1.09 \times 10^{-7}\). Expanding \(\sin\theta\) as a Taylor series and taking its third order expansion, the relative error between the chain and the harmonic approximation is:
\[
\epsilon = \frac{\theta^2}{6} \approx 2.0 \times 10*^{-15}
\]
When we treat the string as a continuum by taking the harmonic approximation, the error in the audible range is right to 15 decimal places. The error only starts to stack up when we push far into inaudible territory like 1,000 modes, 10,000 modes, or higher.
So yea, infinite mode is a fiction, but it’s an extraordinarily good one.






NoteI can’t help it baby. Here’s a probability detour.





For those with experience in probabilistic measure theory, the mass density function is within the same family of functions as the probability density function:
\[
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx
\]
where \(f(x)\) is the density of a probability measure on the Borel sets of \(\mathbb{R}\), and \(\mu(x)\) is the density of a mass measure on the Borel sets of the string, \([0, L]\).
The only difference is in normalization. A mass density integrates to \(M\), while a probability density integrates to 1. Interestingly, if we divide the mass density by \(M\), we recover a pdf:
\[
f(x) = \frac{\mu(x)}{M}
\]
which is the distribution of where a random bit of string’s mass might be located in.
Under this translation, it allows us to reinterpret key physical concepts with familiar statistics:

Center of mass as mean \[
x_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int x\mu(x)\,dx = \mathbb{E}[X]
\]
Moment of inertia about the center of mass as variance

\[
I = \int (x-x_{cm})^2\mu(x)\,dx = $M$Var(X)
\]
As an exercise, you can show that mass is a measure.
Let \(\mu : [0, L] \to [0, \infty)\) be a continuous mass density, and for each Borel set \(B \subseteq [0, L]\) define \[
m(B) = \int_B \mu(x)\,dx
\]

Show that \(\mu\) is Borel-measurable.
Using (a), show that \(m\) is a measure on the Borel sets by verifying the measure axioms, i.e. that \(m(\varnothing) = 0\), \(m(B) \ge 0\), and \[
m\Big(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} B_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} m(B_i)
\] for pairwise disjoint Borel sets \(B_1, B_2,\dots\)

End of detour.

section: Appendix A: The Derivation of The String Formula
text:
Appendix A: The Derivation of The String Formula

Setting the initial boundary conditions
Consider an ideal string of length \(L\) and wave speed \(v\), with displacement \(u(x,t)\) and initial position \(\varphi(x)\). A string under uniform tension, fixed at both ends and released from rest, satisfies
\[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = v^2\dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}, & 0<x<L,\ t>0,\\[1.5ex]
u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0, & t \ge 0,\\[1ex]
u(x,0) = \varphi(x),\quad \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x,0) = 0, & 0 \le x \le L.
\end{cases}
\tag{1}\]
We propose an ansatz of the form \(u(x,t) = X(x)\,\Theta(t)\), where \(X\) is the shape of the string and \(\Theta\) is the scaling of the shape in time.


Separation of variables
With \(u(x,t) = X(x)\Theta(t)\), \[
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = X(x)\,\Theta''(t), \qquad \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = X''(x)\,\Theta(t),
\]
so the wave equation becomes \[
X(x)\,\Theta''(t) = v^2\,X''(x)\,\Theta(t).
\]
Dividing by \(v^2 X(x)\Theta(t)\) wherever it is non-zero, \[
\frac{X''(x)}{X(x)} = \frac{1}{v^2}\,\frac{\Theta''(t)}{\Theta(t)}.
\]
The left side depends only on \(x\) and the right side only on \(t\).

Lemma 1 If \(g(x) = h(t)\) for all \(x\) and \(t\), then \(g\) and \(h\) are equal to the same constant.


Proof. Fix \(x = x_0\). Then \(h(t) = g(x_0) =: a\) for all \(t\). Fix \(t = t_0\). Then \(g(x) = h(t_0) =: b\) for all \(x\). Hence \(b = g(x) = h(t) = a\), and \(g(x) = h(t) = a\) for all \(x, t\).

By Lemma 1, both sides equal a constant \(\sigma\): \[
X''(x) = \sigma X(x), \qquad \Theta''(t) = \sigma v^2\,\Theta(t).
\]
The boundary conditions give \(X(0)\Theta(t) = X(L)\Theta(t) = 0\) for all \(t\). If \(\Theta \equiv 0\) then \(u \equiv 0\), so for a non-trivial solution there is some \(t\) with \(\Theta(t) \neq 0\), and therefore \(X(0) = X(L) = 0\). Thus \(X\) must satisfy \[
X''(x) = \sigma X(x), \qquad X(0) = X(L) = 0.
\tag{2}\]






NoteSturm-Liouville Problem





{#eq-evp} is an example of a Sturm-Liouville problem. Generally on a finite interval \(\left[a,b\right]\), we have: \[
\frac {\mathrm {d} }{\mathrm {d} x}\left[p(x){\frac {\mathrm {d} y}{\mathrm {d} x}}\right]+q(x)y=-\lambda \,w(x)y
\]
Put \(\lambda = \sigma\) and rewrite \(X'' = \sigma X\) as
\[
\frac{\mathrm {d} }{\mathrm {d} x}\left[ X'\right] = -\lambda X, \qquad X(0) = X(L) = 0
\]
This is the Sturm–Liouville form with \(p \equiv 1\), \(q \equiv 0\), \(w \equiv 1\) on \([0, L]\).





The eigenvalue problem
Equation 2 always has the trivial solution \(X \equiv 0\), but that gives \(u \equiv 0\), a string that never moves.
The question is therefore for which values of \(\sigma\) there is a solution \(X \not\equiv 0\). This is an eigenvalue problem: writing \(D = \mathrm{d}^2/\mathrm{d}x^2\) for the operator acting on functions that vanish at \(0\) and \(L\), Equation 2 reads \(DX = \sigma X\), the analogue of \(A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}\) for a matrix. The admissible \(\sigma\) are the eigenvalues and the corresponding \(X\) the eigenfunctions. We treat three possible cases of \(\sigma\) separately and discard cases that leads to the trivial solution of \(X \equiv 0\)
Case 1: \(\sigma > 0\). Write \(\sigma = \mu^2\) with \(\mu > 0\). Trying \(X = e^{rx}\) gives \(r^2 = \mu^2\), so \(r = \pm\mu\), and the general solution is
\[
X(x) = Ce^{\mu x} + De^{-\mu x}.
\]
Since \(\cosh s + \sinh s = e^{s}\) and \(\cosh s - \sinh s = e^{-s}\),
\[
X(x) = (C+D)\cosh\mu x + (C-D)\sinh\mu x = A\cosh\mu x + B\sinh\mu x.
\]
Then \(X(0) = A = 0\), and \(X(L) = B\sinh\mu L = 0\). Since \(\mu L > 0\), \[
\sinh\mu L = \frac{e^{\mu L} - e^{-\mu L}}{2} > 0,
\]
so \(B = 0\) and \(X \equiv 0\).
Case 2: \(\sigma = 0\). Then \(X'' = 0\), so \(X(x) = A + Cx\). From \(X(0) = 0\) we get \(A = 0\), and from \(X(L) = CL = 0\) with \(L > 0\) we get \(C = 0\). So \(X \equiv 0\).
Case 3: \(\sigma < 0\). Write \(\sigma = -k^2\) with \(k > 0\). Trying \(X = e^{rx}\) gives \(r^2 = -k^2\), so \(r = \pm ik\). By Euler’s formula \(e^{\pm ikx} = \cos kx \pm i\sin kx\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
X(x) &= Ce^{ikx} + De^{-ikx} \\
&= (C+D)\cos kx + i(C-D)\sin kx \\
&= A\cos kx + B\sin kx.
\end{aligned}
\]
From \(X(0) = A = 0\), and then \(X(L) = B\sin kL = 0\). A non-trivial solution requires \(B \neq 0\), hence \(\sin kL = 0\). The zeros of \(\sin\) are exactly the integer multiples of \(\pi\), so \(kL = n\pi\), and since \(k > 0\), \[
k = \frac{n\pi}{L}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\]
The eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are therefore
\[
\sigma_n = -\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2, \qquad X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\]


Recovering the time component
With \(\sigma = \sigma_n\), the time equation is
\[
\Theta_n''(t) = \sigma_n v^2\,\Theta_n(t) = -\omega_n^2\,\Theta_n(t), \qquad \omega_n := \frac{n\pi v}{L} > 0,
\]
with general solution \[
\Theta_n(t) = A_n\cos\omega_n t + B_n\sin\omega_n t.
\]
The initial velocity condition gives \(X_n(x)\,\Theta_n'(0) = 0\) for all \(x\), and \(X_n \not\equiv 0\), so \(\Theta_n'(0) = 0\). Since \[
\Theta_n'(t) = -A_n\omega_n\sin\omega_n t + B_n\omega_n\cos\omega_n t,
\]
we have \(\Theta_n'(0) = B_n\omega_n = 0\), and as \(\omega_n > 0\), \(B_n = 0\). Hence \(\Theta_n(t) = A_n\cos\omega_n t\), and each mode is \[
u_n(x,t) = A_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi v}{L}\,t\right), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\]
Mode \(n\) oscillates at frequency \(f_n = \omega_n / 2\pi = nv/2L = n f_1\).


Superposition of the modes
Each \(u_n\) satisfies the wave equation, the boundary conditions and the zero initial velocity. Since these are linear and homogeneous, so does any finite sum of the \(u_n\). We seek the solution as \[
u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos\omega_n t.
\tag{3}\]
At \(t = 0\) this requires \[
\varphi(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right).
\tag{4}\]
For a string plucked to height \(h \neq 0\) at the point \(x = p\), with \(0 < p < L\), the initial position is the triangle \[
\varphi(x) = \begin{cases}
hx/p, & 0 \le x \le p,\\
h(L-x)/(L-p), & p < x \le L.
\end{cases}
\]
To compute \(A_n\), we will make sure of the orthogonality of the modes.

Definition 1 For continuous functions \(f, g\) on \([0,L]\), the inner product is
\[
\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.
\]
If \(\langle f, g\rangle = 0\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are orthogonal.


Lemma 2 For positive integers \(m, n\), \[
\int_0^L \sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L}\right)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\mathrm{d}x =
\begin{cases} 0, & m \neq n,\\ L/2, & m = n. \end{cases}
\]


Proof. By the product-to-sum identity \(\sin a\sin b = \tfrac12\bigl(\cos(a-b) - \cos(a+b)\bigr)\), \[
\sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L}\right)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
= \frac12\left(\cos\left(\frac{(m-n)\pi x}{L}\right) - \cos\left(\frac{(m+n)\pi x}{L}\right)\right).
\]
For any non-zero integer \(k\), \[
\int_0^L \cos\left(\frac{k\pi x}{L}\right)\mathrm{d}x = \frac{L\sin(k\pi)}{k\pi} = 0.
\]
Case \(m \neq n\). Both \(m - n\) and \(m + n\) are non-zero integers, so both cosine terms integrate to \(0\).
Case \(m = n\). Then \(\cos\bigl((m-n)\pi x/L\bigr) = 1\), while \(m + n = 2n\) is a non-zero integer, so
\[
\int_0^L \left(\frac12 - \frac12\cos\left(\frac{2n\pi x}{L}\right)\right)\mathrm{d}x = \frac{L}{2}.
\]



Applying the fourier series
Define \(e_n(x) := \sin(n\pi x/L)\).

Theorem 1 (Convergence of Fourier series) If \(F\) is \(2L\)-periodic, continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable, then its Fourier series converges to \(F\) uniformly on \(\mathbb{R}\).

Let \(F\) be the odd \(2L\)-periodic extension of \(\varphi\). It is continuous, because \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\), and piecewise linear, with corners only at \(x \equiv \pm p \pmod{2L}\). Since \(F\) is odd, its Fourier series contains only sine terms, and on \([0,L]\) it takes the form Equation 4. By Theorem 1, therefore, Equation 4 holds, with the series converging uniformly on \([0,L]\).
Multiply Equation 4 by \(e_m(x)\) and integrate over \([0,L]\). Uniform convergence allows term-by-term integration, so by Lemma 2, \[
\int_0^L \varphi(x)\,e_m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
= \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \int_0^L e_n(x)\,e_m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x
= A_m\cdot\frac{L}{2}.
\]
Hence, \[
A_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \varphi(x)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\mathrm{d}x.
\tag{5}\]


Computing \(A_n\)
Let \(k = n\pi/L\). On each of \([0,p]\) and \([p,L]\), \(\varphi\) is linear, so we may integrate by parts on each piece: \[
\int_0^L \varphi(x)\sin kx\,\mathrm{d}x
= \left[-\frac{\varphi(x)\cos kx}{k}\right]_0^p + \left[-\frac{\varphi(x)\cos kx}{k}\right]_p^L
+ \frac{1}{k}\int_0^L \varphi'(x)\cos kx\,\mathrm{d}x.
\]
The two boundary contributions at \(x = p\) cancel because \(\varphi\) is continuous there, and those at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) vanish because \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\). Therefore \[
A_n = \frac{2}{Lk}\int_0^L \varphi'(x)\cos kx\,\mathrm{d}x,
\qquad
\varphi'(x) = \begin{cases} h/p, & 0 < x < p,\\ -h/(L-p), & p < x < L. \end{cases}
\]
Using \(\sin kL = \sin n\pi = 0\), \[
\begin{aligned}
A_n &= \frac{2}{Lk}\left[\int_0^p \frac{h}{p}\cos kx\,\mathrm{d}x - \int_p^L \frac{h}{L-p}\cos kx\,\mathrm{d}x\right] \\
&= \frac{2}{Lk}\left[\frac{h}{p}\cdot\frac{\sin kp}{k} - \frac{h}{L-p}\cdot\frac{\sin kL - \sin kp}{k}\right] \\
&= \frac{2}{Lk}\left(\frac{h}{p} + \frac{h}{L-p}\right)\frac{\sin kp}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \[
\frac{h}{p} + \frac{h}{L-p} = \frac{h(L-p) + hp}{p(L-p)} = \frac{hL}{p(L-p)},
\]
we obtain \[
A_n = \frac{2h\sin kp}{p(L-p)\,k^2} = \frac{2hL^2}{n^2\pi^2\,p(L-p)}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right).
\tag{6}\]


Proving uniforming convergence of the series
To show that the series is indeed uniform converging and the swapping of integraion and sums in Equation 5 are justified, we apply the Weierstrass M-test on our series. From Equation 6 and \(\left|\sin(n\pi p/L)\right| \le 1\),
\[
|A_n| \le \frac{C}{n^2}, \qquad C := \frac{2|h|L^2}{\pi^2\,p(L-p)}.
\]
Let \(f_n(x,t) := A_n\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos\omega_n t\) denote the terms of Equation 3. Since \(|\sin| \le 1\) and \(|\cos| \le 1\) and \(\sum{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}\), \[
|f_n(x,t)| \le M_n := \frac{C}{n^2} \quad \text{for all } (x,t) \in [0,L]\times[0,\infty),
\qquad
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} M_n = \frac{C\pi^2}{6} < \infty.
\]
For \(N > K\) and every \((x,t)\), \[
\left|\sum_{n=K+1}^{N} f_n(x,t)\right| \le \sum_{n=K+1}^{N} M_n,
\]
so the partial sums are Cauchy at each point and converge to \(u(x,t)\). Letting \(N \to \infty\), \[
\left|u(x,t) - \sum_{n=1}^{K} f_n(x,t)\right| \le \sum_{n>K} M_n \xrightarrow[K\to\infty]{} 0,
\]
and this bound does not depend on \((x,t)\). Hence Equation 3 converges uniformly on \([0,L]\times[0,\infty)\) by the Weierstrass M-test, and \(u\) is continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions.
Every term vanishes at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), so \(u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0\), and at \(t = 0\) the series reduces to Equation 4, so \(u(x,0) = \varphi(x)\). Generally, the displacement \(u(x,t)\) of the plucked string is therefore \[
u(x,t) = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2\,p(L-p)}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi p}{L}\right)\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\cos\left(\frac{n\pi v}{L}\,t\right).
\tag{7}\]

title: An Introduction to Markov Chain Monte Carlo.
text:
Here’s a simple question: “What is the probability that it will rain tomorrow?”



It’s gonna be a wet week.


You might think that this is a no-brainer. Open your weather app and there it is: 75%. But what does that 75% actually mean?
Think about how we usually make sense of probability. When we say a fair coin has a 50% chance of landing heads, we mean that if we flip it hundreds or thousands of times, roughly half the flips will be heads. This is the definition behind the statistics most of us met in Stats 101, with its z-tables and p-values: probability is how often something happens when you repeat it. We call this frequentist probability.






NoteThe frequentist definition of probability





Consider an experiment that can be repeated indefinitely under identical conditions, with each repetition independent of the others. Let \(A\) be an event, and let \(N_A(n)\) be the number of times \(A\) occurs in the first \(n\) repetitions. The frequentist probability of \(A\) is the limiting relative frequency:
\[
P(A) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{N_A(n)}{n}
\]








Proportion of heads over 10,000 flips of a fair coin.




That 50% doesn’t promise a clean half in any particular batch. Ten flips could give seven heads; a thousand might give 480. What it promises is that the more you flip, the closer the proportion drifts toward 50%. On this view, probability is a statement about the long run. That makes it intuitive for coins, dice and cards, where we can repeat the experiment as often as we like.
The problem comes when we try to answer the question from earlier:
“What is the probability that it will rain tomorrow?”
First, tomorrow can happen exactly once. Second, it either rains, or it doesn’t. So not only are there no other tomorrows to be repeated, there is no other answer beyond yes or no. So what does the 75% mean?





Proportion of rainy tomorrows, over all the tomorrows we can observe.




The usual workaround is to rephrase the question:
“What is the probability that it will rain on days like tomorrow?”
But which days count as “like tomorrow”? Days in October? Days with clouds this thick? October days with clouds this thick and wind from the east? Each choice gives a different answer, and theory doesn’t tell you which is right.
Yet, when the app shows 75%, we understand it perfectly well. Think about how we interpret the usual weather report: Nobody pictures a thousand imaginary tomorrows. What we instead think of is how sure we should be that it will rain on the one tomorrow we’re actually going to get.
This is a different idea of probability: it’s a degree of certainty, which involves having a prior knowledge and a certainty that shifts as new evidence comes in. Wake up to dark clouds, and your 75% might creep up to 90%. Check the radar and see the storm veering away, and it drops.
This idea goes back to the 1760s, to an English minister named Thomas Bayes, and was developed further by the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace. Today it carries Bayes’s name: Bayesian probability.



How good is your pastor with mathematics?


For most of its history, though, it had two problems. Critics attacked its reliance on prior knowledge as unscientific. Worse still, the arithmetic became impossible for the problems that mattered, because the computation explodes with every unknown you add. For nearly two centuries, Bayesian methods were confined to the simplest problems and pushed to the margins of statistics.
What brought them back from the grave was a method called Markov Chain Monte Carlo, or MCMC.
To see why it works, we’ll first look at how Bayesian probability turns a hunch into number and evidence into updates. Then why that update becomes hopeless to compute as complexity grows. And finally, how the solution came from an unlikely place: a random walk. Ending with an answer to this unintuitive question:
How could wandering around at random crack a problem that defeated mathematicians for two hundred years?

text:
Making Sense of Bayes
Let’s start small. Forget tomorrow for a moment, and suppose you’ve just moved to a new city at the start of October. You know nothing about its weather and it could very well be anything. I hear you ask: Does it rain seven out of ten days? Or one in ten? Let’s try to answer that.
Call that unknown \(\theta\) (theta): the share of October days that rain, in the long run. It’s a property of the city’s climate, like its average temperature, and seven in ten would be \(\theta = 70\%\).
But there’s a problem when trying to measure the probability of \(\theta\). \(\theta\) is a fixed fact, and to a frequentist a fixed fact can’t have a probability. Either it is 70% or it isn’t. So we have to reinterpret it under a Bayesian view. You don’t know \(\theta\), and that’s uncertainty. Since in Bayesian view, probability is a measure of uncertainty, \(\theta\) can have a probability now.
So what does your uncertainty about \(\theta\) look like? It isn’t a single number. It’s a spread of plausibility over every value \(\theta\) could take. To keep things simple, let’s only consider whole percents: \(\theta\) could be 0%, 1%, 2%, and so on up to 100%. That’s 101 candidates, and your belief is just how much plausibility you give to each one.
Since you genuinely have no idea, the honest place to start is to spread your belief evenly, giving each of the 101 candidates an equal share. This starting belief is called the prior.





Each bar is one of the 101 candidates. As all candidates are equally likely, the prior is flat. Such a graph is also called a distribution.





Updating our prior with evidence
Suppose on the first day of October, it actually rained. How does that change our belief?
We first ask every candidate the same question: if this was the true \(\theta\), how surprised would I be by a rainy day?
If \(\theta = 90\%\), hardly at all, since rain was 90% likely. If \(\theta = 10\%\), quite surprised, since rain was only 10% likely. To put a number on our surprise, we rate each candidate. After a rainy day, each value of \(\theta\) gets a rating of \(\theta\). After a dry day, it gets \(1-\theta\). We call this rating the likelihood: how well each candidate predicted what you actually saw.






TipWhy is it \(1-\theta\) for a dry day?





Each day either rains or it doesn’t, so the two chances must add up to 100%. If rain has a 90% chance, a dry day has a 10% chance. In general, \(P(\text{dry}) = 1 - P(\text{rain}) = 1 - \theta\).



For every candidate, you now hold two numbers: how plausible it seemed before the rain, and how well it predicted the rain. And we combine them to update our belief.
Imagine 10,100 copies of the city, 100 for each candidate, and let the first of October happen in all of them. Where \(\theta = 90\%\), about 90 cities get rain; where \(\theta = 10\%\), about 10 do. Since it did rain, cross out every dry city. The two candidates were tied before, but now \(\theta = 90\%\) is nine times likelier.
Its 90 survivors are \(90/10{,}100 \approx 0.89\%\) of all cities, which is exactly its prior (\(1/101\)) times its likelihood (\(0.9\)). In general, each candidate’s share of surviving cities is prior \(\times\) likelihood, and we call this the unnormalized posterior.





After one rainy day, each candidate keeps prior \(\times\) likelihood of all the cities. \(\theta=0%\) is ruled out as it has no wet days.




There’s one last bit of bookkeeping. These shares don’t add up to 100%. Instead they add up to 50%, as half the cities were crossed out. So this isn’t a belief yet (A probabilty is strictly 0% to 100%). To make it one, divide every share by the total that survived with:
\[
Z = \sum_{k=0}^{100} \text{prior}_k \times \text{likelihood}_k = 0.5.
\]
\(Z\) is called the normalizing constant, or the evidence. It’s the fraction of cities that saw what you saw. Dividing by it gives the posterior:





Updated belief after seeing one rainy day.






A month of weather
Now keep going. On the second of October, your belief after day one becomes the new prior, and the same counting happens again with that day’s weather. Then again on the third, and so on through the month. Each day multiplies in another factor of \(\theta\) or \(1-\theta\). So a month with 23 rainy days and 7 dry ones gives a likelihood of
\[
p(D \mid \theta) = \theta^{23}\,(1-\theta)^{7},
\]
where \(D\) stands for the data, those 30 days of weather. Only the candidates that predicted the whole month reasonably well have cities left. Your belief narrows into a hump around 75%.







The posterior after 30 days. It’s so normal, or is it actually?




Written out, that’s all of Bayes’ theorem:
\[
\underbrace{p(\theta \mid D)}_{\text{posterior}}
= \frac{\overbrace{p(D \mid \theta)}^{\text{likelihood}} \times \overbrace{p(\theta)}^{\text{prior}}}{\underbrace{Z}_{\text{evidence}}}
,
\qquad
Z = \sum_{k=0}^{100} p(D \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k)
\]

NoteThe mathematics behind our calculations.





Setup. The candidates and the flat prior:
\[
\Theta = \{0, 0.01, \dots, 1\}, \qquad \theta_k = \frac{k}{100}, \quad k = 0, \dots, 100,
\qquad
\theta \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\Theta) \;\Rightarrow\; p(\theta_k) = \frac{1}{101}.
\]
The weather on day \(t\) is \(x_t \in \{0, 1\}\) for \(t = 1, \dots, 30\), with \(x_t = 1\) for rain and \(x_t = 0\) for no rain. Given \(\theta_k\), the days are independent and each is a Bernoulli trial, so our likelihood is \(x_t \mid \theta_k \sim \mathrm{Bern}(\theta_k)\):
\[
p(x_t \mid \theta_k) = \theta_k^{x_t}(1-\theta_k)^{1-x_t},
\qquad
p(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid \theta_k) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta_k).
\]
The unnormalized posterior, the normalizing constant and the posterior are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) &= p(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k), \\
Z &= \sum_{k=0}^{100} p(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k), \\
p(\theta_k \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) &= \frac{\tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1, \dots, x_n)}{Z}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Day 1: rain (\(x_1 = 1\)).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Prior:} \quad & p(\theta_k) = \frac{1}{101} \\
\text{Likelihood:} \quad & p(x_1 \mid \theta_k) = \theta_k^{1}(1-\theta_k)^{0} = \theta_k = \frac{k}{100} \\
\text{Unnormalized posterior:} \quad & \tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1) = p(x_1 \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k) = \frac{k}{100} \cdot \frac{1}{101} = \frac{k}{10100} \\
\text{Normalizing constant:} \quad & Z = \sum_{k=0}^{100} \frac{k}{10100} = \frac{1}{10100} \sum_{k=0}^{100} k = \frac{1}{10100} \left( \frac{100 \cdot 101}{2} \right) = 0.5 \\
\text{Posterior:} \quad & p(\theta_k \mid x_1) = \frac{\tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1)}{Z} = \frac{k}{5050}
\end{aligned}
\]
Day 2: rain (\(x_2 = 1\)). Yesterday’s posterior is today’s prior.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Prior:} \quad & p(\theta_k \mid x_1) = \frac{k}{5050} \\
\text{Likelihood:} \quad & p(x_2 \mid \theta_k) = \theta_k^{1}(1-\theta_k)^{0} = \theta_k = \frac{k}{100} \\
\text{Unnormalized posterior:} \quad & \tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1, x_2) = p(x_2 \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k \mid x_1) = \frac{k}{100} \cdot \frac{k}{5050} = \frac{k^2}{505000} \\
\text{Normalizing constant:} \quad & Z = \sum_{k=0}^{100} \frac{k^2}{505000} = \frac{1}{505000} \left( \frac{100 \cdot 101 \cdot 201}{6} \right) = 0.67 \\
\text{Posterior:} \quad & p(\theta_k \mid x_1, x_2) = \frac{\tilde p(\theta_k \mid x_1, x_2)}{Z} = \frac{k^2}{338350}
\end{aligned}
\]
The same posterior also follows from the flat prior and both days at once. Substitute \(p(\theta_k \mid x_1) = p(x_1 \mid \theta_k)\,p(\theta_k)/p(x_1)\), and \(p(x_1)\) cancels:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta_k \mid x_1, x_2)
&= \frac{p(x_2 \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k \mid x_1)}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} p(x_2 \mid \theta_j)\, p(\theta_j \mid x_1)} \\
&= \frac{p(x_2 \mid \theta_k)\, p(x_1 \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k) \,/\, \cancel{p(x_1)}}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} p(x_2 \mid \theta_j)\, p(x_1 \mid \theta_j)\, p(\theta_j) \,/\, \cancel{p(x_1)}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Day \(n\). The prior is \(p(\theta_k \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})\) and the likelihood is \(p(x_n \mid \theta_k)\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
p(\theta_k \mid D)
&= \frac{p(x_n \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} p(x_n \mid \theta_j)\, p(\theta_j \mid x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})} \\
&= \frac{p(x_n \mid \theta_k)\, p(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid \theta_k)\, p(\theta_k) \,/\, \cancel{p(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})}}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} p(x_n \mid \theta_j)\, p(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1} \mid \theta_j)\, p(\theta_j) \,/\, \cancel{p(x_1, \dots, x_{n-1})}} \\
&= \frac{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta_k)\; p(\theta_k)}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} \left( \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta_j) \right) p(\theta_j)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In general, the posterior is
\[
p(\theta_k \mid D) = \frac{L(\theta_k; D)\, p(\theta_k)}{\sum_{j=0}^{100} L(\theta_j; D)\, p(\theta_j)},
\qquad
L(\theta_k; D) = p(D \mid \theta_k) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta_k) \text{ by independence}.
\]
Take \(n = 30\) and we recover our distribution.





From a belief to a forecast
Back to the question we actually care about: will it rain tomorrow given we have observed 30 days of data?
To make a forecast, we treat each candidate as an expert and ask them for the chance of rain. The \(\theta = 60\%\) expert says 60%, the \(\theta = 90\%\) expert says 90%, and so on. However, it would be a mistake to trust all candidates equally because not all of them are equally likely to be right.
To account for this, we rely on the posterior which tells us how much to believe each candidate, given the data. So we weight every expert’s answer by our belief in them. This gets us a new distribution called the posterior predictive distribution. We can then add up all the belief, amd since the weights add up to 100%, we get a weighted average which is our forecast.
\[
P(\text{rain tomorrow at day 31} \mid D) = \sum_{k=0}^{100} \underbrace{p(\text{rain tomorrow at day 31} \mid \theta_k)}_{\theta_k} \; p(\theta_k \mid D) = 0.75
\]





Blue: the posterior, adds up to 100%. Purple: each candidate’s vote for rain, \(\theta_k \times p(\theta_k \mid D)\), adds up to the 75% forecast.










TipWhere the forecast formula comes from?





We write \(\tilde y\) for tomorrow’s weather, day 31. We have that tomorrow’s weather depends on which climate is true, so split over the candidates using the law of total probability
\[
P(\tilde y = \text{rain} \mid D) = \sum_{k=0}^{100} P(\tilde y = \text{rain} \mid \theta_k, D)\; p(\theta_k \mid D)
\]
We treats days as independent given the climate, i.e once you know \(\theta_k\), the past month tells you nothing more about tomorrow. So \(P(\tilde y = \text{rain} \mid \theta_k, D) = P(\tilde y = \text{rain} \mid \theta_k)\).
Like every other day, tomorrow is a Bernoulli trial with success probability \(\theta_k\), so \(P(\tilde y = \text{rain} \mid \theta_k) = \theta_k\).
In general, for continuous \(\theta\):
\[
p(\tilde y \mid D) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid D)\, d\theta
\]



Doing the calculation, we get a forecast that answers our question naturally: Given what we have observed for the past 30 days, there is a 75% chance that it will rain tomorrow.

The forecast is a single number, but the posterior holds far more than that. You can ask it which climates are still plausible, how sure you can be that this is a rainy city, and how many rainy days to expect next week.
Start with the first. To find the range of climates you’re 95% sure contains the true one, cut 2.5% of belief from each end of the posterior. Starting from \(\theta = 0\), add up belief until you reach 2.5%: that’s the lower bound. Keep going until you reach 97.5%: that’s the upper bound. The middle holds 95% of your belief, and here it runs from 59% to 88%.





The 95% credible interval holds the middle 95% of your belief about \(\theta\). The dashed lines mark where cumulative belief reaches 2.5% and 97.5%, at \(\theta\) = 59% and 88%.




The interval is wide, it’s almost 30 percentage point. Well given that we only observed 30 days of weather, being convinced that the city is likely to be rainy but not being able to pin how wet down exactly makes sense.
The interval also means exactly what it sounds like. A 95% credible interval states there’s a 95% probability that \(\theta\) lies betweeen 59% and 88%. This sounds obvious but the confidence interval, that we learned in Stats 101, can’t tell you that.






NoteCredible intervals vs confidence intervals





A 95% confidence interval is a statement about a procedure. If you repeated the experiment many times and built an interval with lower bound \(L(X)\) and upper bound \(U(X)\) each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true \(\theta\). Any single interval you’ve computed either contains \(\theta\) or it doesn’t, so its probability is 0 or 1. What’s random is the interval but \(\theta\) is fixed.
\[
P_\theta\big(L(X) \le \theta \le U(X)\big) \ge 0.95 \quad \text{for every } \theta
\]
A 95% credible interval reverses that. It is a statement about this interval, given this data:
\[
P(0.59 \le \theta \le 0.88 \mid D) = \sum_{k:\ 0.59 \le \theta_k \le 0.88} p(\theta_k \mid D) \approx 0.95
\]
With this method, we find that we have a 95% probability of where \(\theta\) is. The interval is fixed but \(\theta\) is random.
Most people read confidence intervals as if they were credible intervals. With plenty of data and a mild prior, the two are often numerically close, a result known as the Bernstein–von Mises theorem [1], which is why the misreading rarely causes trouble. You would be wrong in principle to read a confidence interval as “\(\theta\) has a 95% chance to be in this interval”, but usually it doesn’t matter. However with little data or a strong prior, they can differ substantially.



Suppose now, you want to know whether this is a city where it rains more often than not. In other words, is \(\theta\) above 50%? The posterior can answer that directly. We add up the belief on every candidate above 50%:
\[
P(\theta > 50\% \mid D) = \sum_{k:\ \theta_k > 0.5} p(\theta_k \mid D) \approx 99.8\%
\]
So you can be practically sure it’s a rainy city. A narrower question, whether \(\theta\) is above 80%, comes out at about 25%: possible, but you shouldn’t bet on it.





Left: belief that \(\theta > 50\%\), the city rains more often than not. Right: belief that \(\theta > 80\%\), the city is very wet. Vertical lines show the cuttoff at \(\theta = 0.5 \text{ and } 0.8\) respectively.




This looks like the question a p-value answers, but it isn’t. A p-value asks: if \(\theta\) were exactly 50%, how often would a month look at least this rainy? Here the answer is about 0.3%.
It’s tempting to read that as “a 0.3% chance the city isn’t rainy,” but that isn’t what it says. The p-value assumes the hypothesis and asks about the data. The posterior does the reverse: it takes the data as given and tells you how plausible the hypothesis is. With it, we can justifiably say there’s a 0.2% chance that the city isn’t rainy.






NoteConfused by p-value? Read this.





A p-value starts from a null hypothesis, \(H_0: \theta \leq 0.5\), against an alternative hypothesis, \(H_1: \theta > 0.5\). It also needs a test statistic, \(T(X)\), the number of rainy days. The p-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of seeing data at least as extreme as what you actually saw:
\[
p = P_{\theta \leq 0.5}\big(T(X) \ge T(x)\big) = \sum_{k=23}^{30} \binom{30}{k} (0.5)^{30} \approx 0.0026.
\]
In other words: if rain really fell on exactly half of October days, a month with 23 or more rainy days would turn up only about 0.26% of the time. That’s well below the conventional threshold of 0.05, so we reject \(H_0\) and conclude the city is quite the rainy one.
Note what p-value doesn’t conclude. It doesn’t say there’s a 0.26% chance that \(\theta = 0.5\), or a 99.74% chance that the city is rainy. It only makes a statement about the data, assuming the hypothesis!

The posterior probability reverses that:
\[
P(\theta \le 0.5 \mid D) = \sum_{k:\ \theta_k \le 0.5} p(\theta_k \mid D) \approx 0.002
\]
Here the data are fixed, and the probability is your belief about \(\theta\). Unlike the p-value, we can say there’s a 0.2% chance that \(\theta \leq 0.5\), or a 99.8% chance that the city is rainy. This is because the posterior makes a statement about the hypothesis, given the data.
The two numbers happen to be close here. For a one-sided question with a flat prior, they often are. But they answer different questions, and they can disagree badly. For a sharp hypothesis such as “\(\theta\) is exactly 50%”, a small p-value can sit alongside a high posterior probability that the hypothesis is true, a result known as Lindley’s paradox [2].
